summary:
FIREFALL is a network where AI agents from different organizations and the people they work with run a spacecraft fire safety review together. A real review already spans several organizations: the vehicle builder, NASA's data archive, a test lab and an independent safety office. In FIREFALL each of them joins with its own agent. The agents talk directly over an agent-to-agent (A2A) network, share answers instead of private data, and use their own tools on their own computers, for example running fire simulations on their GPU farm. When agents disagree, or a decision matters, they escalate to a person. 

An engineer approves the plan, settles disputes and signs the report, and a technician runs the real lab test. For the challenge, the archive's agent turns NASA PSI microgravity combustion data into evidence for a specific cabin. It ranks the relevant studies, processes the raw experiment data, and shows where the evidence runs out. This matters because Artemis habitats and rovers will use oxygen-rich atmospheres in lunar gravity, where materials burn more easily, and every one of them needs a fire safety review.

details:
Live demo: https://firefall.space

Open Source: https://github.com/kaandesu/firefall


What it does

Before a crewed spacecraft, station, lunar base or rover can fly, engineers have to show that a fire on board cannot start, spread or go unnoticed. That review is slow, mostly manual, and spread across several organizations: the team building the vehicle, NASA’s data archives, a test lab, and an independent safety office. Meanwhile almost 20 years of microgravity fire experiments (BASS, Saffire, FLEX, SAME, ACME) sit in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database. Anyone can search them by keyword, but nobody uses them to answer the real question: is my cabin safe at this oxygen level, in this gravity?

FIREFALL answers that question. An engineer hands over the files a team already has: a cabin description (atmosphere, gravity, volume, smoke detectors), a materials list and a simple cabin model. FIREFALL then runs a full fire safety review:

  • It finds the NASA experiments that matter for this cabin. It ranks 20 PSI investigations and 206 real burn tests by how close they are to the cabin’s oxygen, pressure, gravity and materials. It also says plainly where the evidence runs out. For example, no test was ever run above 40 % ambient oxygen.
  • It turns the raw data into numbers you can use. It reads real experiment camera footage and sensor logs and finds ignition, steady burning and extinction automatically. It fits simple models to results published in NASA papers and shows how well they match.
  • It simulates the fire in the cabin itself: how flames spread from part to part, how fast pressure rises, where smoke goes in microgravity, lunar gravity and on Earth, and whether the smoke detectors would catch it. It also runs NIST’s Fire Dynamics Simulator, a standard tool used by fire engineers, on the same cabin.
  • It proposes fixes (swap a material, move the smoke detectors, check whether a CO₂ flood would put a fire out) and backs each one with the data behind it.
  • It writes a hazard report a safety panel can read. An AI chat beside the report answers questions using only what is in the report, and pulls up the chart or test point behind each answer.


How it works

Each organization in a review is represented by its own AI agent: one for the vehicle team, one for the NASA data archive, one for the test lab, one for the safety office. The agents meet on a shared network and work together much like the departments do today. They ask each other questions, hand work over, and disagree when they should.

Two things make this different from one big AI doing everything:

  1. Organizations share answers, not their data. The archive’s agent already knows its datasets, so other agents ask it instead of downloading and re-reading gigabytes of raw files. A company never has to hand over private data such as designs, lab records or supplier information. It only answers the questions it chooses to answer.
  2. People stay in charge. Nothing runs until an engineer approves the plan. When agents disagree (say, the materials expert endorses a change and the safety office objects), the review lead lays out both sides and a person decides. Agents can also hand physical work to people: the lab agent books a real flammability test and a technician runs it. The report stays a draft until a person signs it.

Every question, answer, objection and decision is recorded, so the conversation itself becomes the audit trail a safety review panel wants to see.

The website lets anyone watch a full example review of the Apollo 1 command module in their browser, with no setup. Teams can also connect their own real agents.


Benefits

  • Decades of NASA research put to direct use. Fire experiments from the ISS become evidence in a specific design decision, not just entries in a database.
  • Faster reviews. Work that takes weeks of documents and meetings is laid out on one screen, with each claim linked to its source.
  • Better answers, at lower cost. Asking the organization that owns the data gives a more accurate answer than having every team re-read it. In the example review this avoids reading about 730,000 tokens of raw data.
  • Privacy by design. Companies can collaborate on safety without exposing their intellectual property.
  • Gaps made visible. FIREFALL shows where the evidence stops, so engineers know which tests still have to be run instead of trusting results that don’t apply.
  • Clear accountability. Every decision shows who made it and what it was based on.


Indented Impact

Artemis plans an exploration atmosphere of 34 % oxygen at reduced pressure for lunar habitats and rovers. More oxygen makes materials burn more easily, so much of today’s approved materials list will have to be checked again. NASA has also found that some materials burn at lower oxygen levels in lunar gravity than on Earth. Commercial stations, lunar bases and pressurized rovers will all go through this kind of review in the coming years, and there are only so many fire safety experts.

FIREFALL aims to make those reviews faster, better grounded in real data and easier to check, so that the next crew never meets the kind of fire Apollo 1 did. The same ideas apply on Earth. Smoke too fine for a common detector, and putting out fires by changing the air, matter in closed rooms, vehicles and data centers. The model of organizations working together through agents, without giving up their data, fits any field where safety reviews cross company lines, such as aviation, energy or medical devices.


Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: TypeScript (the whole app and its tools), plus shell scripts for data preparation.
  • Website: React, Vite and Tailwind CSS. React Flow for the agent network and plan, Three.js and Remotion for the 3-D cabin and its animations.
  • Agent collaboration: Lagrange, an open agent-to-agent (A2A) network, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which gives each agent its own set of tools.
  • AI: Claude (through Claude Code) as a connected agent that runs the review tools, and an OpenAI model for the report chat. Claude Code also helped us write the software.
  • Simulation: NIST Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS 6.11.1), plus our own in-browser fire spread, pressure and smoke flow models.
  • Data: NASA PSI datasets (ACME, Saffire-I, BASS-II), results from NASA technical reports (BASS-II, Saffire, FLEX), and the NASA-STD-6001 flammability standard.
  • Hosting: Docker, deployed at firefall.space.
  • Hardware: our own laptops. The fire simulations ran locally on a Mac.


Creativity

  • It treats fire safety as a team conversation, not a search box. The challenge asks for a dashboard that summarizes and ranks research. We built the dashboard into the review where those findings are actually used.
  • Agents stand for organizations, not tasks. Each one keeps its own data, tools and knowledge, just like the real departments and companies do.
  • Humans are part of the network. A technician running a real test and an engineer making a call are part of the same conversation as the agents.
  • The fire happens in the cabin. Simulations play out inside the actual spacecraft model, at three levels of gravity, so a non-specialist can see why a design passes or fails.
  • A report you can question. You don’t have to take the report on trust. You can ask it why, and it shows you the evidence.


What we considered

  • Honesty about what is real. The site clearly marks what is real data and real simulation, and what is illustrative in the example review. Our fire models are meant for screening. They do not replace NASA’s required tests or the safety panel, and we say so.
  • Who would actually use it. We designed for materials and safety engineers at vehicle builders and space agencies, the people who write hazard reports today. We followed the steps they already work through (material tests, configuration analysis, panel review).
  • Data ownership and trust. Real organizations will not upload their designs to a shared system, so the design keeps data inside each organization.
  • Gravity and atmosphere. Fires behave differently in microgravity, on the Moon and on Earth, and at higher oxygen levels. Every result is checked across all three gravity levels.
  • Keeping people responsible. Safety decisions have to have a named person behind them, so the AI proposes and explains, and people decide.
  • Clarity. Engineers are busy. Each screen shows little by default, and the details open on a click.
  • Using real NASA data, processed by code and cited back to its source, rather than numbers typed in by hand.
